## Proof

We wish to evaluate

$$S \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\int_{I}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{(k-1)!}\,t^{\,k-1}\,e^{-\lambda t}\,dt, \qquad I=(a,b),$$

where I write $t$ for the dummy variable $t_k$ since each integral uses the same interval $I$.

**Step 1 — Identify the integrand as a Gamma density.**

For each $k\ge 1$, the function

$$f_k(t)=\frac{\lambda^{k}}{(k-1)!}\,t^{\,k-1}\,e^{-\lambda t}$$

is the density of a $\text{Gamma}(k,\lambda)$ random variable (shape $k$, rate $\lambda$). In particular $f_k(t)\ge 0$ for $t>0$, so the partial sums of the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f_k(t)$ are non-negative and monotonically increasing. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem we may interchange sum and integral:

$$S=\int_{I}\Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{(k-1)!}\,t^{\,k-1}\,e^{-\lambda t}\Biggr)dt.$$

**Step 2 — Sum the series pointwise.**

Factor out $\lambda$ and re-index with $j=k-1$:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{(k-1)!}\,t^{\,k-1}\,e^{-\lambda t}
=\lambda\,e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda t)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}
=\lambda\,e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda t)^{j}}{j!}.$$

The inner sum is the Taylor series of the exponential function, which converges for every real $\lambda t$:

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda t)^{j}}{j!}=e^{\lambda t}.$$

Therefore, for every $t$,

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{(k-1)!}\,t^{\,k-1}\,e^{-\lambda t}
=\lambda\,e^{-\lambda t}\cdot e^{\lambda t}=\lambda.$$

**This is the key identity: the series of integrands sums pointwise to the constant $\lambda$.**

**Step 3 — Integrate the constant.**

Substituting back,

$$S=\int_{a}^{b}\lambda\,dt=\lambda\,(b-a).$$

In particular, when $I=(0,1)$ (a unit interval), $S=\lambda$; more generally the value is $\lambda\cdot|I|$. The essential content — that the **summation (of the series of integrands) equals $\lambda$** — is established in Step 2: the Poisson/Gamma family $\bigl\{\frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!}t^{k-1}e^{-\lambda t}\bigr\}_{k\ge 1}$ forms a partition of unity (up to the constant $\lambda$) because the exponential series collapses the $e^{-\lambda t}$ factor exactly. $\blacksquare$
